style: calm, natural hesitations, like explaining to a friend
slides: Points of view in action. One task, lots of directions.
Should people who don't pay taxes be allowed to vote?
So let's take one task, and run it through the points of view.
A bill proposes to take away the right to vote from people who don't pay taxes. Should non-taxpayers be allowed to vote?
The task already gives us two arguments. Rights come with duties, and voting is a basic right. That's way one. Now let's see how many more we find, just by changing direction.
And one thing before we start. Some of these arguments are better than others. That's fine. The point is to get your head out of the obvious.
Social-economic. The question is, how is money involved here?
First: stronger enforcement, and more people following the rules, means the state collects more tax. More money for the state.
Second: a clear system, with a clear price for not paying, can convince more people to pay their taxes on their own.
Both of these support the bill. So, social-economic doesn't only work against it.
Psychological. How does it affect the way people feel, think, and behave?
A label. Once there's a law, non-taxpayers aren't just people who did the wrong thing. They're bad people. A social stigma.
A toothless penalty, a punishment with no teeth. A lot of the people who don't pay taxes don't vote anyway. So taking away their vote doesn't scare them at all.
And even worse, the law creates a link in people's heads. I don't vote anyway, so why should I bother paying taxes? So the law could actually make people pay less tax. The opposite of what it wants.
Educational. What does it teach? What behaviour does it encourage?
A disconnected punishment. Someone commits a money offence, and loses a political right. A good punishment connects to the offence. This one doesn't, so it teaches nothing about taxes.
And positive versus negative reinforcement. People change their behaviour more through encouragement than through punishment. So, reward the people who pay, instead of punishing the people who don't.
Democracy. Democracy depends on the idea that the majority decides. Stopping parts of the population from voting weakens that idea, and weakens representation.
Rights. Voting is a basic political right of every citizen. A policy that takes it away as a punishment harms that right directly.
And we could go on. Moral: people give to the state in other ways besides tax. Safety: groups with no voice in parliament may look for other ways to be heard.
Look what happened. The task gave us two arguments. And in a few minutes, just by changing direction, we have about ten.
Environment, science and progress? Nothing real here. So we skip them. Not every point of view fits every task. And a forced argument is worse than none.
Now, choose. Not ten arguments. The strongest two or three for your side. Against the bill, for example: the counterproductive link, the disconnected punishment, and majority rule.
And notice which ones are the most original. The toothless penalty, and the counterproductive link. Almost nobody thinks of those. And that's what thinking out of the box looks like.
One last habit. And it's a big one.
When you find an argument that has something general in it, save it. Because general ideas come back, from task to task.

Take the state getting involved in the economy. We met it in the reduced tax. It comes back in taxing big companies to support small shops, in a tax on sweetened drinks, in price controls. And every time, it's the same idea. When the state steps into the market, it can protect the weak... but it can also block competition, and the drive to make things better and cheaper.

And there are more. Who pays? Freedom against protection. Security against privacy. Punishment against reward. The policy that backfires. Can it even be enforced? Short term against long term. A power given today, used by tomorrow's government.
So keep a list. The card after this lesson is a start. With every new task, go through your list. Which of my general ideas fits here? You'll be amazed how often one does.
